title: A Wall Street Firm Modeled Out an AI Crash: S&P 500 Down 30%, $20 Trillion Gone. But Here's What Happens Next
detail:
A Wall Street Firm Modeled Out an AI Crash: S&P 500 Down 30%, $20 Trillion Gone. But Here's What Happens Next
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 10:40 AM CST 6 min read
CRWV
INTC
^IXIC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tech stocks closed out October on Friday with the Nasdaq Composite's worst month since March 2025, and the strain has reached the bond market too. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock plunged 29% in one day, and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), whose bonds came under heavy selling over worries about an AI slowdown and its weak balance sheet, has seen its stock drop 35% over the month.

Those jitters are the backdrop for a recent report in which TS Lombard's Dario Perkins models what happens if the AI investment boom ends. In his scenario, U.S. stocks fall at least 30%, wiping out about $20 trillion in market value. However, the firm's advice is still calm: hold a normal amount of risk through diversified global stocks, don't bet against tech too early, and add government bonds only once strain shows. The firm's working assumption shows a reversal in early 2028, though it says that date could slip. Perkins writes that the recent market wobble may be the beginning of the end or may blow over, and the report does not claim to know which.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The one move: stay invested, stay global, wait for strain

Perkins, managing director for global macro at TS Lombard, says the firm does not know when the boom will end, so its answer is not to try to time it. In the report's words, "Investors can maintain a normal amount of risk via a diversified portfolio of global stocks." The firm argues this bubble differs from the dot-com era because it is "much more concentrated on the U.S. and the AI supply chain," so investors can hold exposure that sidesteps the most concentrated bets.

Bonds come second. TS Lombard says investors "can also add government bonds, but only once signs of fragility emerge." The reasoning comes down to timing. Shorting U.S. tech now, or adding long-dated bonds early, would risk underperforming if the investment boom runs for several more years, with stocks rising and yields drifting higher in the meantime.

The report also expects non-U.S. stocks to outperform over time and argues the dollar is ultimately headed lower.

What a crash could look like

In the scenario, the S&P 500 falls at least 30%, with tech down 40% and other sectors down 20%. That erases about $20 trillion of market value. The report's detailed estimate puts losses on AI-related debt, including private credit, at $125 billion to $190 billion. Perkins said in the report that "the AI crash scenario is now overdetermined. There is just a lot that could go wrong."

The weakest links are AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), stand-alone model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, and construction and equipment suppliers. Hyperscalers, the giant spenders, would face revenue downgrades but are not seen as serious credit risks.

Even so, TS Lombard expects only a mild U.S. recession, comparable to 1990 or 2001. That's because the Fed has room to cut rates, private-sector balance sheets are healthy, and rate cuts would help the lower end of what the report calls America's K-shaped economy. It estimates the crash would cut about 2 percentage points from the level of U.S. GDP. It also estimates that the AI data-center construction boom has created around 500,000 jobs, which could reach 800,000 by the end of 2027.

Sandisk Sinks 13% Last Friday After a Beat: Kioxia Says the Flash Price Surge Is Fading © Lisa Fotios from Pexels and Bigc Studio via Canva

Sandisk (SNDK:NASDAQ) shares fell 13.47% to $1,150.89 on Friday, October 30, a day after the company beat its own guidance and guided above consensus. The trigger came from Tokyo: fab partner Kioxia (285A) guided below estimates and warned the AI-driven surge in flash prices is fading, Bloomberg reported.

The selling ran through the memory chain. Micron (MU:NASDAQ) slid more than 5%, and Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) fell 28.58% after a weak fourth-quarter guide tied to PC demand squeezed by memory costs. Sandisk's own numbers show why Kioxia's warning hit so hard: pricing has stopped doing most of the work.

What Sandisk Reported

Revenue of $11.03 billion, up 23% sequentially, above the $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion guide

Non-GAAP EPS of $49.51 against a $44 to $46 guide

Second-quarter guide of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion, about 12% growth at the midpoint

An 8-for-1 split, with split-adjusted trading from November 20 (no change to value)

Sandisk's Price Engine Is Slowing Fast

Revenue jumped 51% last quarter, and management said about two-thirds came from higher prices. That's roughly 34 points of growth from pricing alone.

SNDK Quarterly Revenue: June 2025-October 2026 (TIKR)

This quarter, CFO Luis Visoso put pricing at about 40% of a 23% gain, or roughly 9 points. He guided only "modest" price increases from here. Consumer revenue fell 29% to $397 million as buyers balked at higher prices, the same squeeze Intel described.

Pricing's contribution shrank by about three-quarters in one quarter.

What the Selloff Already Prices In

The two-day drop of about 18% erased roughly $39 billion of value. Contracts cover about half of fiscal 2027 bits and two-thirds of fiscal 2028, so a large share of volume is already spoken for. Sandisk also bought back about 3.2 million shares for $5 billion, around $1,560 each, about 36% above Friday's close.

Where the Street Sees Sandisk Going
SNDK Quarterly Revenue Estimates: December 2026-September 2027 (TIKR)

Consensus sits at $12.50 billion for the December quarter, then dips 0.8% in March before growing about 8.7% and 7.4%. That's a pause, not a downturn. If Kioxia is right about pricing, the March quarter is where it shows first.

title: Wall Street Braces for More Wild Days in Stocks After Tech Rout

Wall Street Braces for More Wild Days in Stocks After Tech Rout

(Bloomberg) -- The stock market got a long-awaited jolt of volatility late last week after disappointing earnings from technology giants added to angst around the AI-driven rally.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Ray-Ban Heir Rejects $3.9 Billion Offer for Stake in Family Firm

WSJ Wins Dismissal of Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Suit

Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist

Apple Overtakes Nvidia to Become World's Most Valuable Company

Valero to Buy, Restart Idled Texas Refinery as Fuel Rallies

Now traders are bracing for further shocks this week from the US midterm elections and Nvidia Corp. earnings later in November.

The Cboe Volatility Index on Friday touched the highest intraday level since April as the S&P 500 dropped the most since June. The premium for puts protecting against further losses also surged, as did correlations among stocks, which can signal broader stress in the market. Still, those measures remain well below the levels in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran.

With Nvidia due to report earnings, following disappointing results from Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Intel Corp., investors are preparing for more episodes of volatility. Traders are also eyeing US midterm election results for the potential effect on the war in Iran and domestic economic policy.

"This looks more like a bullish rotation with a derating at its core than the beginning of a broad market deterioration.," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Investment Management.

So far, the latest selloff has been largely focused on the technology sector, with investors rotating away from the high-flying firms that led the gains this year. Realized 60-day volatility on the US benchmark last week touched the lowest in more than a year, with the low correlation this year and tendency of zero-day options traders to buy dips and sell rallies helping to restrain moves.

The late-week slide comes in a year that's been relatively placid. While 2025 saw a cluster of extreme market swings around the tariff tumult in April, in 2026 US stocks have largely shrugged off spikes in oil prices and interest rates.

But even as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 capped its worst month since 2025, some investors were betting on a recovery. There were pockets of call and call spread buying seen Friday on the benchmark indexes and some of the most beaten-down tech names such as Intel.

Options were relatively pricey before the larger gyrations late in the week, with the VIX at the higher end of the range over the past five years compared with 20-day realized swings.

Big Tech just had a week investors will remember. At its low on Friday, Alphabet had lost $477 billion in market value for the week, its worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock by Yahoo Finance's calculations, Yahoo Finance reported on October 30.

Most of the damage came Thursday, when the Google parent lost $475 billion in a single session after its third-quarter results. For October as a whole, Yahoo Finance calculated a loss of about $766 billion at Friday's low. That is the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company, behind only SpaceX's roughly $822 billion drop in July.

Heavy Losses Spread Beyond Alphabet

Alphabet wasn't alone. SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week, according to Yahoo Finance. Intel fell as much as 30% on Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades, and Amazon shed about $70 billion after reporting results Thursday. Software stocks took some of the sharpest hits in percentage terms, with ServiceNow and Fortinet down roughly 25% to 33%.

Nvidia was among the biggest losers. Our analysis of whether Nvidia can sustain its exceptional margins as it becomes more than a chipmaker looks at what keeps its profits so high.

UBS Argues Against Heading for the Exits

Not all the money left the market. Eli Lilly, Tesla and SK Hynix added about $370 billion in combined value over the same stretch, even as the Magnificent Seven stumbled, Yahoo Finance said.

UBS's chief investment office argued against retreating. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the bank's CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote on Friday that further volatility does not make leaving markets an effective way to protect a portfolio from drawdowns. She said UBS still sees scope for equity gains overall and believes investors should focus on "building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech."

The selloff also left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade, Yahoo Finance noted. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why Alphabet's low P/E is misleading even as the AI opportunity looks real.

title: Prediction: This Will Be Intel's Stock Price by Year-End 2027
detail:
Prediction: This Will Be Intel's Stock Price by Year-End 2027
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 9:20 PM CDT 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
9984.T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Two years ago, it seemed like nobody wanted to touch Intel (NASDAQ: INTC). The company that basically invented the modern chip industry had turned into its own cautionary tale, posting an $18.8 billion net loss for 2024 while it fell behind Nvidia in artificial intelligence (AI) and behind Taiwan's foundries in manufacturing.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Then something strange happened. The U.S. government bought a stake in Intel. So did Nvidia. So did SoftBank. Companies and governments don't usually hand over billions to a business they think is finished, and that's the real reason I think the next 14 months matter more for this stock than almost any stretch in Intel's recent history.

The chip that actually has to work

Turnarounds aren't real until a real, working product ships, and Intel is finally shipping. In July, the company said its newest Arizona fab had entered high-volume manufacturing on a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 chips, known as Panther Lake, the first processor built on Intel 18A, which Intel calls the most advanced semiconductor process ever developed and manufactured in the United States. Its second-quarter 2026 release adds that the next node behind it, 18A-P, had already entered risk production, meaning Intel isn't just trying to catch up on one generation, it's trying to stay on pace for the one after. On the data center side, that same release says Intel also launched Xeon 6+, its first server chip built on 18A.

Why the smartest money in the room bought in anyway

Money talks, and in 2025 three very different yet massive buyers said the same thing with their wallets. The U.S. government invested $8.9 billion in Intel common stock, structured largely out of unpaid CHIPS Act and Secure Enclave funding, in exchange for roughly 275 million shares and warrants for up to 241 million more. Nvidia added $5 billion, and SoftBank put in another $2 billion, both also in Intel common stock. None of this money really guarantees Panther Lake sells well, or that Intel's foundry business ever turns a real profit. But I think it's an odd thing to do if you think a company is circling the drain, and you don't have any faith in it.

That said, I won't pretend this is a clean story. Intel raised another $20 billion through a common stock offering this past August, priced at $95 a share. A raise that size dilutes existing shareholders even while it shores up the balance sheet. That's on top of the hundreds of millions of shares discussed above already issued to the government, Nvidia, and SoftBank, which means every dollar of future profit gets split more ways than it used to. Retail (the common investor) is getting the short end of the stick.

Intel's updated fair value estimate has been reduced from US$116.37 to US$107.21, a cut of about 7.9% that reflects a more cautious pricing anchor in current models. This shift lines up with the split analyst reaction after Q3 and Q4 guidance, where confidence in Intel's long term AI and foundry plans is balanced against concern about PC weakness, supply issues, and a wide range of ratings and targets. As you read on, you will see how to track these changing views and what they may mean for your own Intel thesis over time.

Analyst Price Targets don't always capture the full story. Head over to our Company Report to find new ways to value Intel.

What Wall Street Has Been Saying
🐂 Bullish Takeaways

Several firms still see upside in Intel, with Evercore ISI, New Street, Tigress Financial, BofA and Mizuho all maintaining higher targets in the US$114 to US$145 range even after some trims. These views often tie to AI driven server demand, progress on 18A manufacturing and foundry scale.

New Street, Northland and KGI Securities upgraded Intel in recent months. Their research points to CPU scarcity, improving execution in data center compute and the Terafab partnership as supportive for longer term growth and foundry utilization.

Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo keep Neutral or Equal Weight stances with reduced targets, yet still highlight potential benefits from AI server demand, advanced packaging traction and eventual visibility on external foundry commitments.

🐻 Bearish Takeaways

A large group of firms including Citi, BofA, JPMorgan, Susquehanna, Jefferies, Wells Fargo and others cut Intel price targets, in several cases quite sharply. Many point to weaker PC demand, client inventory corrections and supply constraints, including the Fab 28 accident in Israel.

Rosenblatt maintains a Sell rating, while Freedom Broker, Roth, Seaport and BofA have moved to more cautious stances. Their research flags delays in Intel's recovery thesis, limited foundry customer traction so far and expectations that manufacturing constraints may cap data center upside.

title: Jim Cramer issues 'falling knife' warning on top chip stock after Intel's outlook
detail:
Jim Cramer issues 'falling knife' warning on top chip stock after Intel's outlook
Mwangi Enos, Celine Provini
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 5:07 PM CDT 5 min read
LRCX
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

One thing trading has taught me is that just because a stock has fallen sharply doesn't mean it can't fall further.

I've watched prices drop to levels that looked attractive, only to see them keep falling. I have learned to be careful and not to rush into a trade simply because something looks cheap.

Jim Cramer offered "Mad Money" viewers a similar warning on Oct. 29, 2026, specifically about Lam Research stock (LRCX).

If you want to buy 100 shares of Lam, I don't want you to buy more than 25 right now. You buy 25, and then you wait another five days because right now the stock is in free fall, and I don't want you to get hurt.

Cramer had nothing but praise for the company itself, calling Lam Research "the best in the game of capital equipment." The warning is about timing, not the business, and the trigger is Intel.

Also Read: Intel CEO reveals a PC problem as Goldman cuts stock target

Intel's bad night became Lam's bad day

"We have some bad numbers from Intel, really bad numbers, and I'm kind of bummed out about it," Cramer said.

Intel reported Q3 fiscal 2026 results on Oct. 29 and guided Q4 revenue to between $15 billion and $16 billion, well short of the roughly $17.1 billion analysts expected.

Non-GAAP EPS guidance is $0.25 compared with a $0.43 consensus. Gross margin is expected to fall to 38% from 44.1%. Client PC revenue is projected to drop more than 20% from $8.1 billion as high memory prices choke PC demand. 

An Oct. 14 fab explosion in Israel, which killed two workers, carries an estimated $300 million hit, with a similar impact expected in Q1. Intel shares fell roughly 30% on Oct. 30 and trade at $63.

More Semiconductors:

Chip stocks set for $229 billion payday before Nvidia ships a GPU

Bank of America makes bold chip call after AI sell-off

Why Richard Ross is buying semiconductors after the AI pullback

I covered Intel in early September when Mizuho reset its price target to $92, and the debate then was whether the AI server story could offset PC weakness.

This quarter answered part of that. Data-center revenue is guided to about $8.4 billion, surpassing PC revenue, but the PC side dragged everything down.

Intel matters to Lam because it buys Lam's etching and deposition tools. When chipmakers begin to tighten budgets, spending on new equipment is often among the first things to slow. 

A strong Lam Research September 2026 quarter that still carried a warning

Lam's own numbers were good. In Q1 fiscal 2027, reported Oct. 21, revenue hit a record $8.22 billion, up 54.4% year over year, beating the $8.14 billion consensus, according to ZACKS.

Intel Sinks 27% in a Week on a Weak Outlook, Despite "Extraordinary Demand" for Its Server Chips ©@Daniel CHETRONI from Daniel Chetroni via Canva, @Vedat OGUZCAN from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel shares fell 27% in the past week on a fourth-quarter revenue guide well short of the $17.1 billion expected.

Data center revenue rose 78%, but substrate shortages and a two-week shutdown at its Israel fab are limiting shipments.

AMD can win server sales Intel can't fill, and the memory shortage lifting Micron is hurting PC demand.

Even after the drop, the stock isn't cheap, with negative free cash flow expected in 2027.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) stock is down 27% in the past week after a fourth-quarter outlook far below Wall Street's.

INTC Stock Price: 1-Week (TIKR)

Friday's 29% drop alone was bigger than the week's loss, after gains earlier in the week.

Rival Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) fell with it, and Intel blamed its PC slump on the memory shortage that's driven record sales at Micron Technology (MU:NASDAQ).

A Strong Quarter, Then a Weak Guide

Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion, with data center revenue up 78% to $7.3 billion.

Then came the outlook:

Revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, against $17.1 billion expected

Adjusted gross margin of 38%, down from 44.1%

Adjusted EPS of $0.25, against a $0.43 estimate

Going in, analysts expected EPS to climb from $0.42 in 2025 to $2.10 in 2027:

INTC Normalized EPS Estimates: 2024-2029 (TIKR)
Plenty of Demand, Not Enough Chips

"Our immediate priority is to unlock additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for our Xeon family," CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in Intel's third-quarter release.

But a shortage of packaging substrates is limiting shipments, and an Oct. 14 explosion that killed two workers at Intel's Israel fab halted production there for about two weeks.

CFO David Zinsner also sees "the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year."

Xeon customers can turn to AMD, and JPMorgan figures Intel's slice of server CPU revenue already went from 77% in late 2022 to 53%. But AMD sells PC chips too, so its report on Tuesday will show whether the PC hit is Intel's alone.

Micron is on the other side of the slump: scarce memory lifted its revenue to a record $54.2 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter, ended Sept. 3.
